label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
**4 out of 5 stars — a real improvement, with a few things to know**

Our congregation paid $2,140 for the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 from Chancel AV in February 2026, plus $95 for the wall mount. That was a substantial purchase for us. We had been livestreaming worship with a webcam since 2020, and I wanted to leave a review for other small parishes trying to decide whether this is worth the money.

For us, it has been. I would buy it again, though I don’t think every small congregation needs to spend this much.

Our nave is 92 feet long, and the camera is mounted on the balcony rail at the back. The 20x optical zoom makes a considerable difference at that distance. We can now show the pulpit or lectern properly rather than asking people at home to make out a small figure at the far end of the church. Delores, who is 82 and homebound, called to say she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That meant more to me than the specifications did.

For those comparing connections, it offers 1080p60, NDI HX and ordinary HDMI output. Power over Ethernet means we only need one cable up to the balcony. Our setup still uses OBS on the old office PC and streams to our YouTube channel, where we generally have 30–60 viewers on Sundays. Buying this camera did not mean replacing everything else.

We have nine presets stored: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide view, and two views of the chancel steps. Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, operates it through the free web app on a tablet. He learned it in one afternoon. I’m a 61-year-old pastor, not an engineer, and I’ve learned more about cameras than I expected to, but the regular Sunday operation is quite manageable.

Getting there was not entirely trouble-free. On the first Sunday, the presets had drifted a few degrees by the sermon. The March firmware update, version 2.4, fixed that for us. The manual is thin and badly translated. Marcy at Chancel AV was excellent on the phone, and that support deserves credit.

Autofocus is another limitation. When someone walks between the camera and the pulpit, it can hunt for focus. We now lock focus on our presets. That works for us, but it is something a new operator should know before worship, not discover during the sermon.

Low-light performance is better than our old webcam, though it is not miraculous. At the Easter Vigil in April, during the first “Christ the Lord Is Risen Today” with only candles, the picture became grainy but remained usable. The old webcam would have shown little more than dots of light. Don’t expect a crisp, bright picture in candlelight, but our people at home could actually see something.

One important warning: this did nothing for our sound problem. Audio is not the camera’s job. If people cannot hear the readings or sermon clearly, a better picture will not solve that, and you should allow for sound work separately.

My rating is **4 out of 5 stars**. It has made worship easier to follow from home, which was the purpose of buying it. The manual, early preset trouble and autofocus behavior keep it from five stars. A congregation under 100 might do perfectly well with something cheaper. For our long nave and the people who depend on our livestream, though, it has been money well spent.
